posts.title: What Black Boys Are Not Allowed to Feel
posts.excerpt: There is a performance tax placed on Black boys before they ever learn to speak. This is me refusing to keep paying it.
posts.content:
There is a performance tax placed on Black boys before they ever learn to speak.

Before we know what grief is, we know what grief looks like when it is suppressed. I started writing at thirteen because the feeling would not fit anywhere else. It went onto the page, because the page asked nothing of me except honesty.

My books are written in the language I was not supposed to learn. They are not performances of strength. They are accounts of what strength actually requires.

Your feelings are not weakness. Your grief is real, and it is allowed to be put somewhere it will not destroy you.

posts.title: The Court and the Page Are the Same Discipline
posts.excerpt: People ask how I balance basketball and writing. I do not. They have never been separate.
posts.content:
People ask how I balance basketball and writing. I do not. They have never been separate.

The same thing that makes you show up to film study when you would rather not makes you sit down with a blank page when nothing is there yet. The discipline is not different. The failure looks different. The patience required is the same.

Basketball taught me to show up when I am empty. Writing required the exact same thing. The practice continues whether the day feels good or not.

posts.title: What I Mean When I Write About Faith
posts.excerpt: Faith in my work is not decoration. It is the wound I keep returning to because it has not resolved.
posts.content:
I did not title a book Our Father? with a question mark to be provocative. I did it because the question was real.

Faith in my work is not decoration. It is the wound. It is the thing I keep returning to because it has not resolved, because it keeps demanding something of me that I do not always have to give.

Where I have landed, at least for now: faith is not a feeling. It is a discipline. It is the daily choice to orient yourself toward something you cannot see but believe has coherence.

posts.title: Seven Books Before Twenty: Why I Could Not Stop
posts.excerpt: I am nineteen. I have seven published books. The real answer is that I could not stop.
posts.content:
I am nineteen. I have seven published books. People ask how.

The real answer is that I could not stop. Not as discipline, though that is part of it, but as necessity. The writing was the only place where the interior life had room to be what it actually was.

Each book came from a specific season and a specific question I was living inside. Seven books means seven rooms I went through. It is not a ceiling. It is a current count.

posts.title: On Love That Does Not Perform
posts.excerpt: I keep writing about love because I keep trying to understand it as practice, not performance.
posts.content:
I keep writing about love because I keep trying to understand it.

Not romantic love specifically, though that is in there. Love as a practice. Love as a discipline. Love without an audience. Love that does not know it is being watched.

Genuine love is expensive. It costs presence, honesty, and time in a way that cannot be scheduled. That is the love I am interested in: not the feeling, but the practice.

posts.title: The Lie I Was Told About Discipline
posts.excerpt: Discipline is not about wanting to. Discipline is about doing it anyway when the return is not visible yet.
posts.content:
Discipline is not about wanting to. That is the lie.

Motivation is unreliable. It comes and goes with sleep and season and whether the last thing you did worked or not. Discipline is what you do in the absence of motivation.

The decision is made once. You show up because you decided to show up, and the showing up is its own justification.
